Arduino · Uno R3 · Lab 15

Real-Time Clock and Daily Routines

Give a desk project a sense of the date and time, then make its reminders behave predictably.

Lab MaterialPracticePractice Quiz

What you will learn

  • Read and deliberately set an I2C real-time clock.
  • Use clock fields for daily windows and date-aware reminders.
  • Distinguish a clock snapshot from elapsed time and stored event history.

On your bench

  • Arduino Uno R3 and USB cable
  • Adafruit DS3231 Precision RTC Breakout, product 3013, with fitted headers
  • LED and 330 ohm resistor
  • Momentary button
  • Breadboard and jumper wires
  • Optional manufacturer-specified 3V CR1220 coin cell for backup only

Meet the components

Recognise the parts in the photos, then follow the labelled task diagrams for connections.

Before you build

  • Upload one task at a time. Disconnect USB power before rewiring; keep D0/D1 available for Serial at 9600 baud. Use this specified 3.3V/5V-compatible Adafruit breakout, not an unidentified DS3231 module with a different battery circuit.
  • The specified breakout has a non-recharging CR1220 holder. No coin cell is needed while USB supplies power. Optional backup uses the specified CR1220 with the holder’s indicated polarity; it keeps the RTC running, not the Uno. Without backup, set the clock again after power loss.
  • In Library Manager install RTClib by Adafruit and its requested dependencies. Wire comes with the Uno core. All times here are a chosen local 24-hour clock; RTClib does not apply time zones or daylight-saving changes.
  • Set the clock with task 1 before the later teaching and practice tasks. Leave it running forward without manual adjustment during a trial. Software reminder/session history lives only in Uno RAM and is cleared by reset; an RTC backup cell does not preserve that history.

Copy one task’s sketch into Arduino IDE at a time. Replace the previous sketch before uploading the next example.

I2C and Clock Initialization

Task 1 · Guided build

Read and deliberately set the desk clock

I2C carries addressed messages over SDA data and SCL clock lines; this RTC uses address 0x68. begin checks whether the device responds. lostPower reads the oscillator-stop flag: if set, the calendar needs verification and setting before these activities use it. A clear flag does not prove that someone entered the correct time. now returns one DateTime snapshot, whose fields stay together even near midnight. adjust changes the hardware clock. The example performs that operation only after an explicit S command, never automatically at startup or from the sketch compilation time. Detection, time validity and application readiness are separate checks. A responding device can contain an unverified calendar, while a lostPower indication is not the same as a missing I2C device. The setting guard allows one deliberate update per run, making accidental repeated Serial characters harmless after that update. A board reset clears this guard but still does not set the clock by itself. Verify the chosen calendar after sending S; correct program logic cannot infer your intended local time from an unset clock.

  1. Connect the four wires shown. Upload and open Serial Monitor at 9600 baud. Without sending anything, observe existing time or the setting message.
  2. Send uppercase S once to apply the supplied Monday test date, 19 April 2027 at 08:29:50. A repeated S is ignored until reset. For real use, edit all six SET_TO fields to a valid chosen local time before uploading and sending S.
  3. Check the printed calendar. Reset the Uno without sending S again: it should read the running RTC, not restore the test time. Reopening Serial Monitor may reset the Uno but must not itself set the RTC.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
// Deliberate test time: Monday, 19 April 2027 at 08:29:50.
// Edit these six fields for another test; sending S applies them once per run.
const DateTime SET_TO(2027, 4, 19, 8, 29, 50);
bool connected = false, clockReady = false, setUsed = false;
unsigned long lastPrint = 0;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  connected = rtc.begin(&Wire);
  if (!connected) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  clockReady = !rtc.lostPower();
  if (!clockReady) Serial.println("TIME NEEDS SETTING");
  Serial.println("Send S once to apply SET_TO; otherwise keep the existing time.");
}
void loop() {
  if (!connected) return;
  if (Serial.available() > 0) {
    char command = Serial.read();
    if (command == 'S' && !setUsed) {
      if (!SET_TO.isValid()) { Serial.println("INVALID SET_TO"); return; }
      rtc.adjust(SET_TO); // Only this explicit command changes the RTC.
      setUsed = true;
      clockReady = !rtc.lostPower();
      Serial.println("TIME SET");
    }
  }
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (clockReady && tick - lastPrint >= 1000UL) {
    lastPrint = tick;
    DateTime stamp = rtc.now(); // One coherent date/time snapshot.
    Serial.println(stamp.timestamp());
  }
}

Observe and check

  • After explicit setting, seconds advance and the date/time prints once per second. Invalid calendar constants are refused.
  • With USB disconnected and no backup cell, later startup may require setting again.

Experiment

  • Explain why copying an old build timestamp into the RTC at every reset would make a desk clock unreliable.

Calendar Fields and Time Windows

Task 2 · Guided build

A weekday reading light

A time window describes a level rather than an event: the LED stays on throughout the interval. Converting hours and minutes to minutes since midnight makes boundaries easier to compare. The start is inclusive and the end exclusive. dayOfTheWeek is computed from the calendar and uses Sunday as zero, so weekdays are one through five. Polling every 250 ms is frequent enough for this minute-based indication without repeatedly querying I2C on every loop pass. The LED is a schedule indicator. A level can be recomputed on every poll without producing duplicate actions: writing the same LED state simply preserves the indication. A notification is different because repeated output is itself an action. Use one snapshot for weekday and minute-of-day so their fields belong to the same instant. The integer minute range fits Uno int, but calculations in seconds over a whole day need a wider intermediate type. Test equality at opening and closing boundaries as well as an ordinary interior time; otherwise an off-by-one comparison can remain unnoticed.

  1. Keep the RTC circuit and add the D5 LED with its 330 ohm resistor. Task 1’s Monday test time lets you approach the first boundary quickly.
  2. Upload this replacement sketch. On Monday through Friday, the light is on from 08:30 through 10:14; at 10:15 it is off. It stays off all weekend.
  3. Use task 1 to set a separate test just before the closing boundary or on a weekend, then return to this sketch. Do not add an automatic clock adjustment to setup.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
bool clockReady = false;
unsigned long lastPoll = 0;
void setup() {
  pinMode(5, OUTPUT); digitalWrite(5, LOW);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!rtc.begin(&Wire)) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  if (rtc.lostPower()) { Serial.println("SET CLOCK WITH TASK 1"); return; }
  clockReady = true;
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (!clockReady || tick - lastPoll < 250UL) return;
  lastPoll = tick;
  DateTime stamp = rtc.now();
  byte weekday = stamp.dayOfTheWeek(); // 0 Sunday; 1 Monday; ...; 6 Saturday.
  int minuteOfDay = stamp.hour() * 60 + stamp.minute();
  bool workday = weekday >= 1 && weekday <= 5;
  bool readingTime = workday && minuteOfDay >= 510 && minuteOfDay < 615;
  digitalWrite(5, readingTime ? HIGH : LOW); // 08:30 included; 10:15 excluded.
}

Observe and check

  • The light switches on at the start boundary and off at the end on a workday. Sunday and Saturday stay off.
  • If initialization or the startup clock check fails, the LED remains off and Serial reports the issue.

Experiment

  • Choose one boundary sample and one weekend sample that would expose a mistaken weekday or interval comparison.

Coherent Snapshots and Date Keys

Task 3 · Guided build

Label a desk log with its whole date

A DateTime object holds one snapshot, so its year, month, day and clock fields can be used together. Calling now separately for each field risks mixing observations across a boundary. Store one snapshot first, then derive every label from that object. The date key year*10000 + month*100 + day identifies a full calendar date rather than merely its repeating day number. On Uno, the UL constants ensure that these products use arithmetic wide enough for an eight-digit key. The key is an identifier, not an elapsed-time value: subtracting date keys does not calculate days between dates. Weekday numbering is another representation, with Sunday zero and Saturday six. A weekday name array can use that index directly if its order matches. Seconds since local midnight likewise need wide multiplication, hour*3600UL + minute*60UL + second; they describe position within one day, not elapsed time across midnight. Choose the representation according to the question.

  1. Upload after deliberately setting a valid clock with teaching task 1.
  2. Compare timestamp, date key and weekday on the same Serial line.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
bool clockReady = false;
unsigned long lastPoll = 0;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!rtc.begin(&Wire)) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  if (rtc.lostPower()) { Serial.println("SET CLOCK WITH TASK 1"); return; }
  clockReady = true;
  lastPoll = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (!clockReady || tick - lastPoll < 1000UL) return;
  lastPoll = tick;
  DateTime stamp = rtc.now();
  uint32_t dateKey = stamp.year() * 10000UL + stamp.month() * 100UL + stamp.day();
  Serial.print(stamp.timestamp());
  Serial.print(" date_key="); Serial.print(dateKey);
  Serial.print(" weekday="); Serial.println(stamp.dayOfTheWeek());
}

Observe and check

  • Every label on a report describes one snapshot.

Experiment

  • Explain why date key 20280301 minus 20280229 is not an elapsed-day calculation.

Combining Calendar Windows

Task 4 · Guided build

Mark two weekend craft breaks

A schedule may combine several time intervals with a day rule. Build small named Boolean conditions before joining them. This weekend example has a morning interval from 10:00 inclusive to 10:15 exclusive and an afternoon interval from 15:00 inclusive to 15:15 exclusive. Either interval qualifies, but only Saturday or Sunday qualifies as a day. Parentheses make that relationship visible: weekend AND either time interval. Without a clear grouping, a later edit could accidentally allow one interval on every weekday. The D5 LED represents the current schedule level and is driven off outside the permitted windows. Startup also begins off, and failed initialization leaves it there. Polling is separate from the calendar rule; the same predicate can be tested with paper timestamps without waiting for a real weekend. These examples assume a valid local clock moving forward and do not apply automatic daylight-saving corrections.

  1. Reuse the RTC and D5 LED circuit and upload this replacement sketch.
  2. Use task 1 for a deliberate boundary test, then return to this sketch.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
bool clockReady = false;
unsigned long lastPoll = 0;
void setup() {
  pinMode(5, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(5, LOW);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!rtc.begin(&Wire)) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  if (rtc.lostPower()) { Serial.println("SET CLOCK WITH TASK 1"); return; }
  clockReady = true;
  lastPoll = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (!clockReady || tick - lastPoll < 250UL) return;
  lastPoll = tick;
  DateTime stamp = rtc.now();
  byte weekday = stamp.dayOfTheWeek();
  int minuteOfDay = stamp.hour() * 60 + stamp.minute();
  bool weekend = weekday == 0 || weekday == 6;
  bool morning = minuteOfDay >= 600 && minuteOfDay < 615;
  bool afternoon = minuteOfDay >= 900 && minuteOfDay < 915;
  digitalWrite(5, weekend && (morning || afternoon) ? HIGH : LOW);
}

Observe and check

  • Both intervals share the same weekend restriction.

Experiment

  • Test a Monday at 15:05 and explain which condition excludes it.

Calendar-Safe Arithmetic

Task 5 · Guided build

Check intervals across date boundaries

Date fields are useful labels, but arithmetic on their pieces quickly becomes fragile. A twelve-second interval can cross midnight, a month boundary, a leap day or a year boundary. This data-only sketch constructs three example DateTime values and adds a TimeSpan of twelve seconds. It does not initialize or adjust the hardware RTC. The resulting DateTime handles calendar rollover within the library’s supported 2000–2099 range. Subtracting complete unixtime values then verifies the elapsed seconds. The subtraction assumes a later valid finish rather than an unsigned backward clock jump. Do not use it while manually correcting the hardware clock during a session. Also distinguish a duration’s total seconds from its seconds component: the component repeats every minute. This example uses one-second resolution, so it cannot describe subsecond reaction time. Explicit boundary examples make calendar assumptions visible without waiting overnight or changing the real clock for every arithmetic check.

  1. Upload this Serial-only calculation sketch; it never sets the RTC.
  2. Compare all three boundaries and their elapsed totals.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
const DateTime starts[] = {
  DateTime(2028, 2, 28, 23, 59, 55),
  DateTime(2027, 12, 31, 23, 59, 55),
  DateTime(2027, 4, 30, 23, 59, 55)
};
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  for (byte i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
    DateTime finish = starts[i] + TimeSpan(12);
    uint32_t elapsed = finish.unixtime() - starts[i].unixtime();
    Serial.print(starts[i].timestamp());
    Serial.print(" -> "); Serial.print(finish.timestamp());
    Serial.print(" seconds="); Serial.println(elapsed);
  }
}
void loop() {}

Observe and check

  • Each case represents twelve seconds despite different calendar changes.

Experiment

  • Explain why subtracting 7 minus 55 does not measure these intervals.

Observed Events and Remembered Identity

Task 6 · Guided build

Announce the first observed date

A clock condition can remain true across many polls. To turn observations into occasional messages, remember the identity of the last reported item. This sketch reports the first observed date and then reports only when a different full date is sampled. Repeated samples on that same date produce no new line. The program does not need to observe exactly midnight: a first sample at 00:00:03 still belongs to the new date. If several dates pass while the sketch is not observing, it reports only the current date and does not fabricate records for missed days. That is an explicit observation policy, not an alarm-recovery mechanism. The date marker lives in RAM, so a reset can produce another report for the same date even if the RTC kept perfect time. With several independent daily reminders, each reminder would need its own last-reported identity; one shared date marker could incorrectly suppress a later reminder on the same day.

  1. Upload and observe the initial date line followed by silence within that date.
  2. Use a deliberate later-date test only between runs, keeping each trial forward-moving.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
bool clockReady = false;
unsigned long lastPoll = 0;
uint32_t lastDate = 0;
void setup() {
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!rtc.begin(&Wire)) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  if (rtc.lostPower()) { Serial.println("SET CLOCK WITH TASK 1"); return; }
  clockReady = true;
  lastPoll = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (!clockReady || tick - lastPoll < 1000UL) return;
  lastPoll = tick;
  DateTime stamp = rtc.now();
  uint32_t dateKey = stamp.year() * 10000UL + stamp.month() * 100UL + stamp.day();
  if (dateKey != lastDate) {
    Serial.print("OBSERVED DATE "); Serial.println(dateKey);
    lastDate = dateKey;
  }
}

Observe and check

  • Missing the instant of midnight does not prevent recognizing a new date.

Experiment

  • Explain why one shared last-date variable cannot represent two independent daily reminders.

Change-Only Status Reports

Task 7 · Guided build

Keep a desk-status log quiet

A current state and a state-change message are different outputs. The LED is written from the current condition every poll, while Serial reports only the first observed state and later changes. The haveState flag makes the initial report explicit, including an initial closed state. Without that flag, initializing previousOpen to false would suppress the first closed report and leave a reader unsure whether sampling had started. This task defines a weekday desk window from 13:00 inclusive to 14:00 exclusive. Repeated in-window samples maintain the LED without filling the log. A delayed poll reports the state it actually observes; it does not reconstruct every transition that may have occurred during a long gap. That limitation should accompany a status log if later analysis depends on exact transition times. Keep the stored state, output pin and reporting policy together when reviewing the logic, while retaining one coherent RTC snapshot per poll.

  1. Upload using the RTC and D5 LED circuit.
  2. Compare the first closed-state report with repeated closed polls and a later boundary change.
Arduino sketch · guided example
#include <Wire.h>
#include <RTClib.h>
RTC_DS3231 rtc;
bool clockReady = false;
unsigned long lastPoll = 0;
bool haveState = false, previousOpen = false;
void setup() {
  pinMode(5, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(5, LOW);
  Serial.begin(9600);
  Wire.begin();
  if (!rtc.begin(&Wire)) { Serial.println("RTC NOT FOUND"); return; }
  if (rtc.lostPower()) { Serial.println("SET CLOCK WITH TASK 1"); return; }
  clockReady = true;
  lastPoll = millis();
}
void loop() {
  unsigned long tick = millis();
  if (!clockReady || tick - lastPoll < 250UL) return;
  lastPoll = tick;
  DateTime stamp = rtc.now();
  byte weekday = stamp.dayOfTheWeek();
  int minuteOfDay = stamp.hour() * 60 + stamp.minute();
  bool open = weekday >= 1 && weekday <= 5 && minuteOfDay >= 780 && minuteOfDay < 840;
  digitalWrite(5, open ? HIGH : LOW);
  if (!haveState || open != previousOpen) {
    Serial.println(open ? "DESK OPEN" : "DESK CLOSED");
    previousOpen = open;
    haveState = true;
  }
}

Observe and check

  • An initial false state is still reported once.

Experiment

  • Describe which transitions cannot be reconstructed after a long sampling gap.

Reset and Backup Boundaries

Task 8 · Explore and measure

Distinguish a running clock from remembered history

An RTC and the Uno do not share the same memory lifetime. Use the unchanged observed-date sketch from teaching task 6 for this experiment. While USB remains connected, press the Uno reset button and compare the new report with the continuing RTC calendar. The sketch’s lastDate variable starts over, so the same calendar date can be announced again. The RTC does not need an automatic adjust call to resume reading. Keeping USB connected makes this experiment independent of whether a backup coin cell is fitted. The optional CR1220 belongs only in the specified non-recharging holder with its marked polarity. It can support the clock during a supply interruption, but it does not run the Uno loop or preserve its ordinary variables. A lostPower flag indicates that the oscillator stopped now or earlier; it is not a current battery-health measurement. Record which device was reset or lost power before drawing conclusions from repeated reminder messages.

  1. Upload teaching task 6 unchanged, keeping USB and all wiring connected.
  2. Press Uno reset once and compare the date output before and after.

Observe and check

  • A duplicate application message can occur while the hardware clock kept advancing.

Experiment

  • Explain why adding a backup cell cannot by itself suppress duplicates after an Uno reset.
